title: Partial Indexes and Filtered Workloads
learningObjectives: Define a partial index and explain how its WHERE condition limits indexed rows.
Create a partial index for a frequently queried subset.
Use a compatible query predicate to benefit from a partial index.
Explain how updates can add or remove rows from a partial index.
Recognize that partial-index support and matching rules vary by DBMS.

understand.concept: A partial index contains entries only for rows that satisfy a WHERE condition in the index definition. It can reduce index size and write maintenance when queries frequently target a subset such as active records or open events.
understand.whyItMatters: Partial indexes can improve performance and reduce storage when a workload repeatedly filters for a well-defined subset of rows.
understand.analogy: An index is like a sorted lookup guide that points toward the relevant records instead of requiring every page to be read.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model B-tree pages, query planner estimates, index maintenance or the full range of SQL access paths.

explain.narrative:
## Partial indexes
A partial index adds a WHERE clause to CREATE INDEX. Only rows satisfying the condition are represented in the index. Queries that use a compatible predicate can benefit from it.

## Design considerations
The query predicate must be compatible with the partial-index condition for the optimizer to use the index. Rows outside the condition are not indexed by that partial index. Updates that move rows into or out of the condition still require index maintenance.

## Portability
Partial or filtered index syntax and optimizer rules differ across database products. The examples target SQLite; verify the feature and predicate matching in the selected DBMS.

### Predicate compatibility
The optimizer must be able to establish that the query predicate implies the partial-index WHERE condition. A query that does not restrict to open events cannot use this index to find all qualifying rows because closed rows are absent from it.

### Portability and maintenance
SQLite supports partial indexes; other products may call the feature filtered indexes or implement different predicate restrictions. Updates that change event_status can add or remove index entries, so partial indexes still have write-maintenance costs.

examples.title: Create an event table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE perf15_events (event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event_status TEXT NOT NULL, created_at TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates an events table with a status and date-like text value. ISO-formatted YYYY-MM-DD values sort lexicographically in chronological order for this fixed format.

examples.title: Insert open and closed events
examples.explanation: Inserts five events: three open and two closed. The partial index created next contains only the three rows whose status is open.

examples.title: Create an index only for open events
examples.code: CREATE INDEX idx_perf15_open_created ON perf15_events(created_at) WHERE event_status = 'open';
examples.explanation: Creates a partial index on created_at restricted to open events. Rows with status closed are omitted from this index, reducing its size when open events are a subset of the table.

examples.title: Inspect the partial-index query plan
examples.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT event_id FROM perf15_events WHERE event_status = 'open' AND created_at >= '2026-02-01';
examples.explanation: Displays the plan for a query whose WHERE clause includes the partial-index predicate and a date range. SQLite may use the partial index because the query condition implies event_status = 'open'; plan details depend on statistics and engine version.

examples.title: Return open events in the date range
examples.code: SELECT event_id, created_at FROM perf15_events WHERE event_status = 'open' AND created_at >= '2026-02-01' ORDER BY created_at;
examples.explanation: Returns the two open events on or after 2026-02-01, ordered by date. This verifies the business result separately from the index access strategy.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and explain why only open events are represented by the partial index.
practise.independentTask: Create a task table with open, closed and archived statuses. Add a partial index for open tasks and write a matching query with a plan check.
hints: A partial index has a WHERE clause in CREATE INDEX.
Only rows satisfying the index predicate are included.
The query should use a compatible predicate.
Rows can enter or leave the index when their data changes.
Check support and syntax in the target database product.

options: An index that includes only rows satisfying a condition
An index with half a column name
An index that cannot be used in WHERE
A temporary table
questions.answer: An index that includes only rows satisfying a condition
questions.explanation: A partial index stores entries only for rows matching its WHERE condition.

questions.prompt: Where is the partial-index condition written?
options: In the WHERE clause of CREATE INDEX
In the SELECT list only
In COMMIT
In the table's primary key
questions.answer: In the WHERE clause of CREATE INDEX
questions.explanation: SQLite partial indexes use WHERE in the index definition.

questions.prompt: Which query is most likely to use an index for open events?
options: A query whose predicate includes event_status = 'open'
A query that filters only unrelated columns
A query that drops the table
A query with no FROM clause
questions.answer: A query whose predicate includes event_status = 'open'
questions.explanation: The query predicate should be compatible with the partial-index condition.

questions.prompt: What happens when an indexed row changes from open to closed?
options: It no longer qualifies for the partial index and the index is maintained
It remains indexed forever
The table is deleted
The index becomes a primary key
questions.answer: It no longer qualifies for the partial index and the index is maintained
questions.explanation: Partial index membership changes as row values change.

questions.prompt: Are partial indexes identical across every DBMS?
options: No, syntax and optimizer matching rules can differ
Yes, every DBMS implements them identically
They exist only in spreadsheets
They cannot be used with WHERE
questions.answer: No, syntax and optimizer matching rules can differ
questions.explanation: Always verify partial or filtered index behaviour in the target product.
